sections.h2: What the Tuscarawas County Recorder does
sections.html:
The Tuscarawas County Recorder keeps the land records for every parcel in the county, and New Philadelphia is the county seat. Each document that conveys or encumbers land gets a permanent record, is stored in archival form and stays open to the public. Fees the office collects go into the county general fund.

Every filing is indexed, and that index is what lets a title searcher string the documents into a chain of title. The chain shows past owners and any debt that still rides with the land. Your buyer's title agent will run that search before closing, so a clean record helps a sale move along.

The county also holds registered land, called Torrens land, and the recorder handles those certificates of title. Most house sales involve ordinary deeds. If your parcel carries an older registered certificate, tell the title company early so it can examine that record.

The recorder lists the per-page rate and the notation rate together at the top of its page. The statute behind those figures is Ohio Revised Code 317.32. Each fee splits into a base amount and a housing trust fund amount, and a preservation surcharge can be added on top.

Tuscarawas County Recorder fees
ChargeAmount
First two pages of a document$39
Each additional page$8
Each marginal notation$4
Non-conforming document$20 extra

Certified copies, plats and other services carry their own statutory rates. Ask the office what applies before you send payment.

The recorder sorts its filings by type. A home seller will run into these most often:

  • Deeds of every kind, including warranty, survivorship, quit claim and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgage papers such as releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and waivers of priority.
  • Land contracts, easements and leases, plus certificates of transfer and affidavits.
  • Plats and condominium drawings.
  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement, along with federal, personal-property and workers' compensation liens.
  • Military discharges, powers of attorney and trust records.

The page ends with a fair housing notice. Under federal law, a deed provision that restricts the sale, rental or use of a dwelling on protected grounds is void and unenforceable.

sections.h2: Getting a deed approved before it is recorded
sections.html:
In this county the auditor's side of the courthouse reviews a deed before the recorder sees it. Start at the auditor's office in the Courthouse Annex, 125 E. High Avenue, New Philadelphia. Posted hours are weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30. The auditor's Deed Conveyance and Transfers section lays out the procedure step by step, with a conveyance requirements form and a separate procedure for mineral deeds.

  • The GIS and Map Office checks the deed against the tax maps. It takes deeds for pre-approval by email, using the surface Conveyance Form, the Mineral Conveyance Form, or both.
  • The auditor's office completes the transfer and collects the conveyance and transfer fees.
  • The recorder's fees are paid when the deed is filed.

The auditor sets the conveyance fees and the per-parcel transfer charge, so call the deed transfer staff for current rates before you write the check. A county may also adopt a transfer tax under section 322.02, capped at 30 cents on each $100 of value. The buyer files the value statement required by section 319.202, and the conveyance fee falls on the seller.

Yes, you can. Since January 20, 2026 the recorder has accepted all document types by eRecording. Conveyance documents add a step: the submitter uploads the pre-approval forms and supporting papers first, beginning with the document type, and only then sends the conveyance itself.

Five eRecording providers are approved: CSC, Hopdox, Indecomm Global Services, ERecording Partners Network and Simplifile. Closing agents normally hold those accounts, so most sellers leave the electronic filing to the title company or attorney.

Records can be searched through the county's cloud search, and the recorder posts instructions for registering an account and setting up a property alert. Ask the office how an alert works before you count on it to watch your parcel. There are two search tools, a cloud search site with quick and advanced modes and a separate county index site, so it can help to check what each one shows for your parcel.

sections.h2: Maps and surveys from the GIS and Map Office
sections.html:
The GIS and Map Office keeps the county tax parcel maps and sells printed copies. A first county road map is free and each extra one costs $1. A plat book of all 22 townships is $25. Tax maps are priced by size:

  • 8.5 by 11 inches: $0.50 without a photo, $1 with one.
  • 11 by 17 inches: $1 without a photo, $2 with one.
  • 18 by 24 inches: $2 without a photo, $4 with one.
  • 24 by 36 inches: $4 without a photo, $6 with one.
  • 36 by 48 inches: $6 without a photo, $8 with one.

Surveys are filed by location and old tax map page. Surveys from 2014 on are online through the parcel viewer. Older ones sit in drawers in the map office while scanning continues as time allows. If a buyer asks for a survey of your lot, look there before you pay for a new one.

The $20 non-conforming charge refers to the state formatting standard in section 317.114, which sets type size, margins and ink color. Have the closing attorney confirm the deed meets it before filing.

sections.h2: Selling a rural or older parcel
sections.html:
Tuscarawas County has a visible Amish and Mennonite community, and plenty of rural land. For a rural parcel, ask the title company to check easements and any recorded survey. Homes here have a median value of $185,400, and 68.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so most buyers you meet will be people who plan to live in the house.

Before you set a price, ask the auditor for the parcel's county value and ask the title company for the last recorded deed. Those two papers tell you what the county thinks the property is worth and who held title before you.

sections.h2: Steps from signed deed to recorded deed
sections.html:
Here is the order most sellers follow once a buyer is lined up.

  • Have the deed drafted and checked against the formatting standard so no $20 charge applies.
  • Email the deed and the right conveyance form to the GIS and Map Office for pre-approval.
  • Take the approved deed to the auditor's office, pay the conveyance and transfer fees, and get the transfer completed.
  • File with the recorder, usually by eRecording through the closing agent, and pay the recording fee.

If you sell for cash, you skip the lender's paperwork, but the deed still goes through the same approval and recording steps. Allow time for each stop and call ahead if the deed is unusual, for instance one that involves minerals.

faqs.q: What does recording a Tuscarawas County deed cost?
faqs.a: Expect $39 for pages one and two and $8 for every page after that. A marginal notation adds $4, and a deed that fails the formatting standard adds $20. The auditor bills the conveyance charge separately.

faqs.q: Do I need pre-approval before recording a Tuscarawas County deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The GIS and Map Office and the auditor approve deeds before the recorder files them. The map office takes deeds by email, and mineral conveyances use their own form and procedure.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed electronically in Tuscarawas County?
faqs.a: Yes. The recorder accepts every document type through eRecording as of January 20, 2026. Conveyance documents must upload the pre-approval forms and supporting papers before the deed is submitted.

faqs.q: Where is the Tuscarawas County Auditor's deed desk?
faqs.a: The auditor's office is in the Courthouse Annex at 125 E. High Avenue in New Philadelphia, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Its website has a Deed Conveyance and Transfers page.

faqs.q: Does the Tuscarawas County Recorder handle registered land?
faqs.a: Yes. The office files certificates of title to registered (Torrens) land. If your parcel carries one, tell your title company early so it can examine the registered record.
